skills.summary: Android rules for Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, condensed from 17 Google and community skills.
skills.description: Android house rules for native Kotlin and Jetpack Compose apps, condensed from 17 Google and community Android skills into one. Covers the app's shape (feature api and impl modules, a Route and Screen split, one StateFlow per screen, repositories as the error boundary), Compose state, effect and list traps, Navigation 3, edge-to-edge insets and the keyboard, adaptive layouts for foldables and tablets, Retrofit with kotlinx.serialization, Coil, Hilt, AGP 9 build logic, tests and preview screenshots, and intent and permission security. Use for any Android work, such as writing or reviewing Kotlin, Compose screens, ViewModels, Gradle files or AndroidManifest.xml, fixing jank, inset or state-loss bugs, or Jetpack Compose questions in general.
skills.body:
Android rules for a Kotlin and Compose app, in one place. Each rule corrects a mistake agents make.
Basics they already get right are left out.

`<skill-dir>` below is the folder holding this file. Claude Code exposes it as `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`.

**The project wins.** Read the repo's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` first. Where it disagrees with this
skill, follow the project and say so once. In existing code, find the mechanism that's already there
(the effect stream, the error type, the navigator) and widen it instead of adding a second one.

## Working rules

- Don't run builds, tests, installs or emulators unless the user asks. Finish the code, then hand over
  the exact commands (`./gradlew :app:installDebug`, `./gradlew testDebugUnitTest`) and what to try.
- When asked to build: one Gradle build at a time, never `clean`, never `--stop`, never in the
  background. Use the device the user names. A physical phone beats an emulator on a small Mac.
- Versions live only in `gradle/libs.versions.toml`. Check a new version on Google Maven or Maven
  Central before writing it. Never take one from memory.
- Crashes: `adb logcat -d -b crash`. Never log tokens, one-time codes or payment details.

## Default stack

When the project hasn't chosen yet:

| Concern | Default |
| --- | --- |
| UI | Jetpack Compose, Material 3, one Activity, edge-to-edge |
| Navigation | Navigation 3 (`NavDisplay`, `@Serializable` keys) |
| State | `ViewModel` with one `StateFlow`, coroutines. No `LiveData` or RxJava in new code |
| DI | Hilt with KSP. Assisted injection for per-screen arguments |
| Network | Retrofit, OkHttp, the kotlinx.serialization converter |
| Images | Coil 3 `AsyncImage` |
| Storage | Room, DataStore for preferences |
| Build | AGP 9 with built-in Kotlin, convention plugins in `build-logic`, one version catalog |
| Tests | JUnit4, Robolectric, Compose UI tests (v2 APIs), Roborazzi or Compose Preview Screenshot Testing, Turbine |

## App shape

```text
:app                  MainActivity, DI roots, manifest, the routing table
:core:model           backend types and the one Json config (pure JVM, no Android)
:core:common          Loadable, DataError
:core:network         Retrofit services, networkCall {}
:core:data            repositories (the error boundary), caches, session
:core:designsystem    theme, components, ScreenInsets
:core:navigation      Navigator, one back stack per tab, scene strategies
:core:testing         MainDispatcherRule, JSON fixtures
:feature:x:api        NavKeys and navigateToX() helpers, nothing else
:feature:x:impl       screens and ViewModels
```

- **Features never depend on another feature's `impl`.** They navigate with the other feature's NavKey
  from `:feature:x:api`. The app module is the only place that maps keys to screens.
- **Lowest visibility that compiles.** `private`, then `internal`, then `public` only for a real
  caller in another module. A public interface's implementation stays `internal`, bound in DI.
- **A screen is two composables.** `XRoute` gets the ViewModel, collects state and effects, and does
  navigation and hand-offs to other apps. `XScreen` is pure: state in, callbacks out, previewable.
  Children get data (`EventCard(event)`), never the ViewModel.
- **One `StateFlow<XUiState>` per ViewModel.** Anything loaded uses `Loadable`:

  ```kotlin
  sealed interface Loadable<out T> {
      data object Loading : Loadable<Nothing>
      data class Loaded<out T>(val value: T) : Loadable<T>
      data class Failed(val error: DataError) : Loadable<Nothing>
  }
  ```

- **Durable outcomes are state. One-shot commands are effects.** If losing the signal would leave the
  person unsure what happened (a payment result, a saved form), it's a `UiState` field the UI clears
  after showing it. Navigation, haptics and scroll-to-top go through
  `Channel<XEffect>(Channel.BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow()`, collected in `XRoute` inside
  `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)`. Not a `SharedFlow`, which drops events while nobody collects.
- **Derived values are getters on the state class** (`val canSubmit get() = emailValid && !isSubmitting`),
  never constructor parameters, so `copy()` can't make them disagree with their inputs.
- **Repositories are the error boundary.** They return `Result<T>` with a `DataError` failure.
  ViewModels never see OkHttp, Retrofit, Room or DTO types (`references/data.md`).
- **Every new response gets a JSON fixture and a decoding test.**

## Compose traps

The full list with code is in `references/compose.md`. These bite most often:

1. Every changing value read inside `remember`, `LaunchedEffect`, `DisposableEffect`, `produceState`,
   or the `remember` around `derivedStateOf`, is in the key list or read through
   `rememberUpdatedState`.
2. Framework state (`LazyListState`, `ScrollState`, `PagerState`, `FocusRequester`, `Animatable`,
   `SnackbarHostState`) stays in the composable. Never in the ViewModel: animations run on the
   composition's clock.
3. A UI value that drives a repository call (a search query) lives in the ViewModel, which debounces it.
4. Effects are UI work. Network calls and database writes belong to the ViewModel.
5. The click is the event. Launch from the handler with `rememberCoroutineScope()` instead of setting a
   flag that a `LaunchedEffect` watches.
6. Typed input and toggles use `rememberSaveable`. Scroll positions use `rememberLazyListState()` and
   `rememberScrollState()`, never `remember { LazyListState() }`, which forgets on rotation.
7. Lazy lists: a stable primitive `key` and a `contentType` on every item, `itemsIndexed` instead of
   `indexOf`, no `SubcomposeAsyncImage` or `BoxWithConstraints` in items, and no impression logging from
   a `LaunchedEffect` in an item (items compose before they're visible).
8. Fast-changing reads (scroll offset, animation values) go in lambda modifiers: `Modifier.offset { }`,
   `graphicsLayer { }`, `drawBehind { }`. They skip composition.
9. Never write state that was already read earlier in the same frame, like `onSizeChanged` writing a
   size that composition reads. Measure the two together in a custom `Layout`.
10. Don't add `@Stable`, `@Immutable` or `ImmutableList` on a hunch. Strong skipping already covers it,
    and annotating a model that holds collections makes each recomposition pay an `O(n)` `equals`.
11. A reusable composable takes `modifier: Modifier = Modifier`, applies the caller's modifier first, and
    hard-codes no outer padding or size on its root.
12. Current APIs: `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`, `mutableIntStateOf`, `Modifier.animateItem()`,
    `PullToRefreshBox`, foundation `HorizontalPager`, `Modifier.Node` for custom modifiers, the
    `LifecycleStartEffect` family. Accompanist is retired.

## Navigation 3

Setup, tabs, sheets, results and deep links with code: `references/navigation.md`.

- Keys are top-level `@Serializable` classes implementing `NavKey`. They carry ids, never callbacks,
  `@Composable` lambdas or whole models.
- One back stack per tab (`rememberNavBackStack` each), plus a stack of visited tabs. All of them
  survive process death.
- ViewModels never hold the back stack. They emit an effect and `XRoute` calls the navigator.
- Passing `entryDecorators` replaces the defaults. List `rememberSaveableStateHolderNavEntryDecorator()`
  first, then `rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator()`.
- Wrap navigating clicks in `dropUnlessResumed { }` so a double tap doesn't push twice.
- A screen returns a result through the result event bus (`LocalResultEventBus`, `ResultEffect<T>`),
  not a shared ViewModel.
- Sheets, dialogs and list-detail are scene strategies chosen by entry metadata. `NavDisplay` animates
  between entries, so don't wrap entry content in `AnimatedContent`.

## Insets and the keyboard

Right and wrong pairs: `references/layout.md`.

- `enableEdgeToEdge()` before `setContent` in every Activity, and
  `android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize"` on Activities with text input. Never
  `android:configChanges` or a locked `screenOrientation` to dodge recreation.
- Apply insets once. A Scaffold's `innerPadding` goes into a list's `contentPadding`, never a
  `Modifier.padding` on the list's parent, which clips content that should scroll behind the bars.
- Scaffold's default `contentWindowInsets` has no keyboard in it. On text-field screens use
  `contentWindowInsets = WindowInsets.safeDrawing` with no `imePadding()`, or the default plus
  `imePadding()` placed before `verticalScroll()`. Both together pad twice.
- Adaptive scaffolds (`NavigationSuiteScaffold`, list-detail scenes) don't pass padding down. Each
  screen applies its own insets. Never pad the suite itself.
- With a bottom bar, set `window.isNavigationBarContrastEnforced = false`.

## Adaptive layouts

- Decide wide layouts by the window size class or the container's constraints, never by device type.
  On screens with text input decide by width only, because the keyboard changes the height.
- `NavigationSuiteScaffold` gives a bar on phones and a rail when wide.
- A vertical list becomes `LazyVerticalGrid(GridCells.Adaptive(minWidth))` when an item reads well at
  that width.
- Check phone, foldable and tablet previews in portrait and landscape.

## Data and network

Code for all of these is in `references/data.md`.

- Retrofit functions are `suspend` and return the body type. `Response<T>` only when you need the
  status, headers or error body.
- One `Json` for the app: `ignoreUnknownKeys = true`, `coerceInputValues = true`,
  `explicitNulls = false`. Every enum has an `Unknown` entry and every enum property defaults to it.
  Lists of things people typed into the backend decode lossily: a bad item drops out, not the screen.
- Keep the backend's field names. Fields are nullable with defaults unless the backend always sends
  them. Say in a comment whether an amount is in major units (rupees, dollars) or minor (paisa, cents).
- Auth goes in an OkHttp interceptor, never a per-endpoint `@Header`.
- **Sign out only when the server refuses the token in its own JSON error.** Never on no signal, a
  timeout, a 5xx, a 429 or a captive portal page, so saved tickets and drafts survive bad networks.
- Rethrow `CancellationException` before any broad `catch`.
- Coil's `AsyncImage` sizes itself. `rememberAsyncImagePainter` needs an explicit `.size()`.

## Build (AGP 9)

Migration steps: `references/build.md`.

- AGP 9 compiles Kotlin itself. Never add `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` or `kotlin("kapt")`. Use KSP,
  and `com.android.legacy-kapt` only for a processor that has no KSP support.
- `kotlin { compilerOptions { } }` at the top level, not `kotlinOptions`.
  `androidComponents { onVariants { } }` instead of `applicationVariants`.
- `buildFeatures { buildConfig = true }` in any module with custom `BuildConfig` fields.
- KSP 2.3.6 or newer, Hilt 2.59.2 or newer.
- Module build files apply convention plugins and set a `namespace`, nothing else. SDK levels, Compose,
  the JVM toolchain and lint live in `build-logic`.
- Check a build change with `./gradlew help` and `./gradlew build --dry-run` before a real build.

## Tests

Shapes and traps: `references/testing.md`.

- Pick the smallest test that proves the behaviour.
- ViewModels and repositories get unit tests with fakes, not mocks. Pass the `MainDispatcherRule`'s
  dispatcher into `runTest(...)` so both share one scheduler.
- Compose UI tests use the v2 APIs (`androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4.v2.createComposeRule`) and find
  nodes by text, content description or role before `testTag`.
- Previews double as screenshot tests. Every `@Preview` renders `XScreen` from fixture state, with no
  Hilt, ViewModel or network.
- A bug fix comes with a test that failed because of the bug.

## Security

Patterns: `references/security.md`.

- `android:exported="false"` on every component that doesn't need outside callers. Exported ones
  validate every extra.
- `PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE` by default, always with an explicit component.
- Never launch an Intent that came from outside without checking its resolved component against an
  allowlist and stripping URI-grant flags (`IntentSanitizer`). Give `onNewIntent` the same checks as
  `onCreate`, and call `setIntent(intent)` first.
- Ask for a runtime permission in context, right before the feature needs it. Explain after a denial,
  and offer app settings once it's permanent. The photo picker needs no storage permission.
  Foreground location first, background later, never in one request. Check permission state each
  time instead of caching it.

## UX defaults

Unless the project says otherwise:

- Errors show inline, where they happened. No toasts or snackbars for errors. Success is the screen
  changing plus a haptic. Dialogs only when something blocks or destroys.
- Every text field sets `keyboardOptions` (type, IME action) and its autofill content type (email,
  new password, one-time code).
- Light and dark from day one. Type from `MaterialTheme.typography`, colours from the scheme.
- Touch targets at least 48dp.

## Reviewing Android code

Report findings as `file:line`, most severe first, in this order:

1. Architecture: a feature importing another feature's `impl`, a ViewModel passed to a child
   composable, DTOs or network exceptions reaching a ViewModel, `public` that could be `internal`.
2. Correctness: missing effect keys, state written during composition, a swallowed
   `CancellationException`, sign-out on a network error, an enum with no `Unknown`.
3. Lifecycle: `collectAsState` on Android, framework state in a ViewModel, state lost on rotation or
   process death.
4. Insets and the keyboard, then adaptive layout.
5. Performance, only with evidence from a list, an animation or a trace.
6. Tests: a new response with no fixture, a fix with no test that failed first.

## References

| Read | When |
| --- | --- |
| `references/compose.md` | writing or reviewing composables, state, effects, lists, performance |
| `references/navigation.md` | Navigation 3 setup, tabs, sheets, results, deep links, list-detail |
| `references/layout.md` | edge-to-edge, the keyboard, adaptive layouts, foldables, saved state |
| `references/data.md` | repositories, Retrofit, JSON models, sessions, Coil, Room |
| `references/build.md` | AGP 9, convention plugins, the version catalog |
| `references/testing.md` | test shapes, Compose test traps, screenshots |
| `references/security.md` | intents, PendingIntent, providers, permissions, credentials |

For anything not covered, prefer Google's current docs (`android docs search "<topic>"` when the
`android` CLI is installed) over memory.

skills.name: blueprint
skills.summary: Turns a plan into an interactive HTML approval gate before you write code.
skills.description: Turn a text plan into ONE self-contained interactive HTML blueprint reviewed before you code — collapsible steps with reuse/reversibility tags, pan/zoom architecture diagrams whose nodes click through to the relevant section, editable+runnable code playgrounds, file maps, data/API blocks, a risk heatmap, a decision log, wireframes, and reviewer annotations that export back to the agent. Zero dependencies: no MCP, no server, no account; works offline and is shareable as a single file. Use BEFORE implementing work that should be reviewed, compared, or approved — multi-file, ambiguous, risky, or UI-heavy changes — and when an existing text/Markdown plan needs a richer review surface. Skip for trivial one-line fixes. (Prism suite; pairs with `replay`.)
skills.body:
Produce a structured, reviewable **blueprint** as a single self-contained HTML file the user
opens in a browser, comments on, and approves — *before* any code is written. The blueprint is the
approval gate and the source of truth, not the chat.

The artifact is **interactive in the browser**: architecture diagrams pan/zoom and their nodes can link
to the section they describe; code snippets can be **editable + runnable** playgrounds; reviewers
annotate any block and export the notes back to you. All in one file, no server.

Unlike hosted planning tools, this skill has **no external dependency**: the artifact is one HTML
file with the structured plan model embedded as JSON inside it. That file is at once the
human-viewable document, the machine-readable model (you re-read it to apply feedback), and a
portable thing the user can commit to the repo or send over chat. It works offline forever.

## When to use / skip

**Use it** whenever a plan is better as a reviewable artifact than a chat paragraph: multi-file or
multi-step work, ambiguous or risky changes, a UI surface with states, an API/data-shape decision
that needs alignment, or when an existing text plan needs a richer review surface.

**Skip it** for truly trivial, unambiguous work — typos, one-line fixes, a single well-specified
function. Just make the change. Never pad a plan with filler and never ship a single-step plan.

## Workflow

1. **Research first — never invent.** Read the real files, schemas, actions, and patterns. Name
   actual files, symbols, and data shapes. For each step, lead with what it **reuses** (existing
   functions, components, schema) before what it **adds**. Delegate wide exploration to a subagent
   when the surface is large. Planning is **read-only** — make no source edits until the user approves.

2. **Decide the hard-to-reverse bets first.** For backend/data/API work, call out decisions that are
   expensive to undo once callers or data depend on them — wire format, public ids, data-model shape,
   auth/ownership boundaries — and get those right in the plan. Capture each as a `decision` block with
   its reversibility flag. Then scope the smallest first cut that proves the approach; state what's in
   and what's explicitly deferred.

3. **Read the block catalog.** Open `references/BLOCKS.md` (relative to this skill) for the authoritative
   block vocabulary and the model schema. Author from it, not from memory — unknown block types render
   as an error box.

4. **Author the model JSON.** Build a `{ "kind":"plan", ... }` model (see schema below). A good plan is:
   - **Outcome-first**: `summary` says what changes and why, in product terms, before mechanics.
   - **Spined on `steps`**: each step has a status (`planned` to start), `reuses`/`adds`/`files`, and a
     `reversibility` flag where it matters.
   - **Concrete near the top**: for UI/product work lead with a `wireframe` of the real app state; for
     architecture lead with one `diagram` and wire its nodes to the relevant sections via `links`. Add
     `datamodel`/`api` blocks next to the prose that needs them.
   - **Lean on interactivity where it pays**: give an architecture `diagram` `links` so reviewers click a
     node to jump to its section; make the one tricky algorithm an `editable`+`runnable` `code` block so
     they can poke at it. Don't sprinkle these everywhere — use them on the thing worth exploring.
   - **Honest about risk**: include a `risk` heatmap for non-trivial work, and a single `questions` block
     near the bottom for anything genuinely unresolved (decide what you can; recommend a default for the rest).
   - **Lean, not thin.** A handful of focused blocks, no filler.

5. **Build the artifact.**
   ```bash
   python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/build.py plan-model.json -o PLAN.html        # lean (diagrams shown as source)
   python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/build.py plan-model.json -o PLAN.html --fetch-mermaid   # offline diagram rendering
   ```
   Write the model JSON next to where the user wants it (e.g. `plans/<slug>/plan-model.json`) and the
   HTML beside it. Keep the JSON — it's the editable source you'll patch on feedback.

6. **Surface it and request approval.** Give the user the absolute path to the `.html` file and tell
   them to open it (the file opens directly in any browser — no server). Name which files/areas the
   work will touch. Presenting the plan and asking for sign-off **is** the approval step — don't ask a
   separate "does this look good?". Do not start coding until they approve.

7. **Apply feedback via the model, not the chat.** Reviewers turn on **✎ Annotate**, click any block to
   leave a note, then **⧉ Copy** (or **⬇ JSON**) to hand the notes back to you. Read those notes, edit
   `plan-model.json`, and rebuild. The document — not the chat — stays the source of truth. Re-read the
   approved plan before major implementation steps.

## Self-review before handoff (high-stakes plans only)

For architecture/backend/data/migration/multi-file plans, run one quick adversarial pass after building:
spawn a skeptical subagent whose only job is to find what's weak, missing, or wrong — unanchored steps,
a hard-to-reverse decision made implicitly, a menu of options where the plan should commit, single-step
filler. Apply clear fixes to the JSON yourself and rebuild; route genuine judgment calls into the
`questions` block. Skip this for small or single-decision plans.

## Model schema (quick reference)

See `references/BLOCKS.md` for the full catalog. Skeleton:

```jsonc
{
  "kind": "plan",
  "id": "stable-slug",
  "title": "Imperative one-liner",
  "subtitle": "optional context",
  "meta": { "repo": "...", "branch": "...", "author": "...", "date": "YYYY-MM-DD" },
  "summary": "Outcome-first markdown.",
  "blocks": [
    { "type": "metrics", "items": [ /* scope at a glance */ ] },
    { "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Approach" },
    { "type": "steps", "items": [ /* the spine; reuses/adds/files/reversibility */ ] },
    { "type": "decision", "choice": "...", "reversibility": "hard", "alternatives": ["..."], "rationale": "..." },
    { "type": "diagram", "title": "Architecture", "mermaid": "flowchart LR ..." },
    { "type": "risk", "items": [ /* blast radius */ ] },
    { "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Open questions" },
    { "type": "questions", "items": [ /* decide what you can; recommend defaults */ ] }
  ]
}
```

## Rules

- **Grounding:** real files/symbols/data only; redact secrets (`sk-•••`). Read before you draft.
- **Read-only until approval.** No edits to source while planning.
- **The document is the source of truth.** On scope change, update the model JSON and rebuild — don't
  only pivot in chat. Keep one bottom `questions` block for the unresolved.
- **When the artifact looks wrong, fix the renderer/skill** (`scripts/template.html`), never hand-edit
  one output `.html`. Turn feedback into better guidance.

skills.name: cross-model-review
skills.summary: Has a different model (Codex by default) review a change in a loop until it runs out of real objections. Panel mode runs three.
skills.description: Has a different model review a change and loops until it runs out of real objections. Runs the Codex CLI read-only as the reviewer when it's installed (else another provider the harness offers, else a fresh subagent), keeps a ledger of findings by severity, fixes the real ones with the smallest change, pushes back on the rest with evidence, and stops after three rounds. Say panel for a panel of reviewers from different providers with scores out of 10. Use when the user says cross-model review, second opinion, cross-check, review with codex, or panel review, or when pr-ready asks for a review.
skills.body:
Hand the diff to a reviewer that didn't write it and doesn't share your blind spots, then argue it
out. The goal is a correct change at its intended
size. A reviewer's approval at any cost isn't.

## Pick the reviewer

In this order:

1. The Codex CLI (`codex` on `PATH`): a different model family, run read-only.
2. Another provider the harness exposes, such as T3 Code's `delegate_task`, a Gemini CLI, or a
   subagent set up to run another provider's model.
3. A fresh subagent of your own model, given only the brief. Say in the report that it's the same
   model family, so a weaker check.

If the user named a reviewer, use only that one. If it isn't reachable, say so instead of
substituting.

## Budget

- Three rounds. Round 1 reviews the whole change; later rounds only the code that changed and the
  findings still open.
- Up to five only for security, auth, payments, data loss or concurrency, while a blocker or
  should-fix stays open with evidence, or when the user asks.
- Stop early when a round returns only nits. Declined nits and comment or formatting fixes need no
  new round.
- One reviewer per round (panel mode aside). The reviewer never starts its own subagents.

## 1. Scope

- `git status --short`. Don't stash, discard or include unrelated changes. If the change's paths
  don't separate cleanly from other work in the tree, stop and ask.
- Find the base after `git fetch origin`. On a PR: `git merge-base HEAD origin/<base>`. Local work:
  `git merge-base HEAD origin/<default-branch>`. Uncommitted work only: `HEAD`.
- Use one diff command for every round: `git diff <base> -- <paths>`, plus untracked files.
- Write the intent and what's out of scope in two sentences.
- Run the checks that cover the change before round 1. Don't send code that doesn't build. Note
  checks that were already failing on the base.

## 2. The brief

Write it to a scratch file:

```text
Review only. Don't edit files, commit, push, comment on GitHub, or start subagents.
Repo: <absolute path>   Base: <sha>
Intent: <one or two sentences>
Out of scope: <list>
Checks run: <command> -> <result>
See the change with: git diff <base> -- <paths>   Untracked files to read: <list>
Read the surrounding code and the callers. Find bugs, broken callers, and mismatches with the intent.
Skip style unless it hides a bug. Hold the change to its smallest form: flag code, tests or guards
the intent doesn't need.
Severity: blocker = the intended case is wrong. should = a real bug callers will hit, within the
intent. nit = anything else (other paths, rare cases, small performance costs, extra compatibility).
Reply in exactly this shape:
VERDICT: APPROVE or CHANGES
H1 [blocker|should|nit] <file>:<line> <claim>. Fix: <suggestion>
Keep ids stable across rounds.
```

## 3. Run a round

```bash
codex exec -s read-only -C <repo> -o <scratch>/review-round-1.md - < <scratch>/review-brief.md
```

- `-s read-only` stops it from writing; `-o` saves its final message. Pass `-m <model>` only when
  the user named one.
- It can take minutes. Run it in the background and wait for it to finish. Don't poll, and don't
  start a second reviewer.
- Don't edit the files under review while it runs.
- A timeout, an error or an empty reply is not approval. Retry once, then report the blocker.

For the subagent fallback, give it the brief and nothing else: not your reasoning, not your
conclusion.

## 4. Answer the findings

Check each finding and its severity yourself. Another path, a rare case or a small cost is a nit
whatever label it came with.

| Your call | Do |
| --- | --- |
| agree | the smallest fix. Prefer deleting or narrowing code over a new lock, cache, helper or option. Add one focused test that fails without the fix when the intent needs it |
| disagree | say why, with evidence: file:line, a test, command output |
| out of scope, or a nit | decline in one line and list it as a follow-up |

Keep a ledger in a scratch file: id, severity, outcome (`fixed`, `disagree`, `declined`), evidence.
Never agree just to end the loop. After fixing, rerun the checks and `git diff --shortstat <base>`.
If the review grew the diff, cut before the next round.

## 5. The next round

Run one only if budget remains and a blocker or should-fix is open, behaviour code changed, or the
last approval doesn't cover the current diff. Send the round 1 brief, the ledger, the same diff
command, and what changed since last round. Ask the reviewer to mark each old id `resolved` or
`still open: <reason>` and to look only at changed code and open ids.

## 6. Stop

Stop when you agree: APPROVE on the current diff, no blocker or should-fix open, and no concern of
your own.

Stop when you're stuck: an item is still disputed after two replies, or the budget ran out. Show both
sides in two or three lines each and let the user decide. Running out of budget is not approval.

Don't push during the loop. Push afterwards only if the user asked to push, ship or update the PR.

## Report

Rounds run, the reviewer (the model name the tool reports, or "not exposed"), the final verdict,
diff size before and after, each finding with its outcome and reason, follow-ups, and whether you
pushed. Put a review line in a PR description only if the repo's conventions allow naming agent
tools there.

## Panel mode

When the user asks for a panel, run three reviewers from different providers in parallel, for example Codex, a Claude subagent and a Gemini CLI, each with the same brief plus
"Score the change out of 10."

- All read-only. Don't edit while any of them is still reading the checkout.
- Don't wait idle: check each result against the code as it lands, and plan fixes while the others
  run.
- A full pass by all three is one round. Fixes start a fresh round.
- Loop until every reviewer is satisfied or the budget ends, still fighting scope growth.
- If fewer than three providers are reachable, say which ran. Never invent a score; write
  `no score`.

```markdown
| Reviewer | Round 1 | Round 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex (model as reported) | 7/10 | 9/10 |
| Claude subagent | 8/10 | 9/10 |
| Gemini | no score | 8/10 |
```

skills.name: ios-swiftui
skills.summary: SwiftUI rules for iPhone apps on iOS 26+ and Swift 6, from a shipping app and the top SwiftUI skills.
skills.description: SwiftUI house rules for native iPhone apps on iOS 26 and later with Swift 6, built from a shipping app's lessons and the best public SwiftUI skills. Covers app shape (a local Swift package of feature modules that never import each other, a router per tab, an Observable screen model holding a Loadable), state ownership and Observation traps, view identity and list performance, navigation, sheets and alerts, Swift 6.2 concurrency with main actor by default, Liquid Glass and iOS 27 toolbars, iPhone Duo and foldable layouts, lenient JSON decoding, Swift Testing, accessibility, and deprecated APIs to replace. Use for any SwiftUI or iOS work, such as writing or reviewing Swift views, models, Package.swift or concurrency code, fixing layout, state or performance bugs, adopting Liquid Glass, or SwiftUI questions in general.
skills.body:
SwiftUI rules for a native iPhone app, in one place. Each rule corrects a mistake agents make. What
they already get right is left out.

`<skill-dir>` below is the folder holding this file. Claude Code exposes it as `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`.

**The project wins.** Read the repo's `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md` first. Where they
disagree with this skill, follow the project and say so once. In existing code, reuse the mechanism
that's there (the router, the loading type, the API client) before adding a second one.

**Current platform facts.** iOS 26 (Liquid Glass) and iOS 27 have shipped, with Xcode 27 and Swift
6.2. Don't dismiss their APIs as speculative. This skill assumes an iOS 26 deployment target: no
`#available(iOS 26, *)` gates or material fallbacks. Gate iOS 27 and 27.1 APIs with `#available`.
If the project's minimum is lower, gate iOS 26 APIs too. Treat the installed SDK as the authority.

## Working rules

- Don't run builds, simulator tests or device installs unless the user asks. Finish the code,
  type-check what you can without a full build, then hand over the exact `xcodebuild` and
  `xcrun devicectl` commands and what to try.
- When asked: the physical device the user names, not a simulator, unless told otherwise. Never run
  tests alongside a device build. Run only the test targets you touched.
- Package tests can't run on a device ("Tool-hosted testing is unavailable on device destinations").
  They need a simulator or CI.
- Xcode 27's simulator app is DeviceHub. There is no `Simulator.app`.
- Screenshots of the user's phone capture whatever is on it. Ask first.

## App shape

```text
App target              FooApp.swift and Assets only
Packages/FooKit
  Models                Codable types matching the backend, one folder per domain   (nonisolated)
  Networking            APIClient, Endpoint, token store, Endpoints/<Domain>.swift  (nonisolated)
  AppCore               config, session, router, Loadable, caches                   (main actor)
  Brand                 fonts, colours, marks; extension-safe for widgets           (main actor)
  DesignSystem          components on top of Brand                                  (main actor)
  SharedUI              domain components several features use                      (main actor)
  <Name>Feature         one module per area; depends on core modules only           (main actor)
  AppFeature            composition root: tabs, the routing table, services
```

- **Features never import each other.** To open another feature's screen, push a `Destination` (or
  present a `SheetDestination`) through the router in the environment. One view in `AppFeature`
  maps destinations to screens.
- **Isolation per module** in `Package.swift`: UI modules get `.defaultIsolation(MainActor.self)`;
  `Models` and `Networking` stay nonisolated. Turn on `NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault`,
  `InferIsolatedConformances` and `MemberImportVisibility` everywhere. Plain value types in UI
  modules that must work off the main actor are marked `nonisolated`.
- **Extension safety.** Modules linked into widgets and intents never touch `UIApplication`, image
  pipelines or anything an app extension can't use.
- **Data flows one way.** View, then an `@Observable` screen model holding a `Loadable`, then
  `api.send(XEndpoints.y)`, then a `Models` type. Views never build URLs or decode JSON.

  ```swift
  nonisolated public enum Loadable<Value> {
      case idle, loading, loaded(Value), failed(String)
      public var value: Value? { if case .loaded(let v) = self { v } else { nil } }
  }
  ```

- **A new screen** is a folder in its feature (`OrderDetailView.swift`, plus `OrderDetailModel.swift`
  if it holds state) and a `Destination` case if other screens open it.
- **A new backend call** is a static `Endpoint` in `Networking/Endpoints/<Domain>Endpoints.swift`
  with its types in `Models/<Domain>/`, plus a JSON fixture and a decoding test.

## State: who owns what

Details and code: `references/state.md`.

1. The view that creates a model owns it: `@State private var model = Model()`, or seeded once in
   `init`. Never `let model = Model()` in a view; it's rebuilt on every parent update.
2. `@State` is always `private`. A non-private `@State var store = Store()` builds a new `Store` each
   time the parent re-renders.
3. A child that only reads takes `let model: Model`. One that needs bindings takes
   `@Bindable var model`. From the environment: `@Environment(Model.self) private var model`, then
   `@Bindable var model = model` inside `body`.
4. Never put changing parent input in `@State`; it keeps the first value forever. Use `let`, or
   `@Binding` when the child writes.
5. No `Binding(get:set:)` in `body`. Bind to a key path or a writable computed property.
6. `@AppStorage` and `@SceneStorage` never go inside an `@Observable` class. They compile and never
   update the view.
7. Observation tracks what `body` reads. Pass a row its element, not the store and an index. Make
   observed property types `Equatable` so equal writes don't invalidate.
8. **Never write `prop?.a = prop?.b` on an `@Observable` class property.** The write begins before the
   read, and the exclusivity check aborts the app. Copy to a local, change it, store it once.
9. Custom environment values use `@Entry`, with stable defaults (no `Model()`, `Date()` or `UUID()`)
   and no stored closures. Keep fast-changing values (scroll offset, geometry) out of the
   environment.

## Views: identity and performance

Details: `references/views.md`.

1. Split big bodies into `View` structs, not computed `some View` properties or `@ViewBuilder`
   functions. Those share the parent's invalidation.
2. `init` stays cheap. It runs on every parent update: no decoding, formatting or filtering.
3. `ForEach` identity comes from the element's stable id. Never `.indices`, `\.offset`, an id made of
   editable fields, or a `UUID()` minted in `body`. `ForEach(items.enumerated(), id: \.element.id)`
   needs no `Array(...)` on iOS 26.
4. Rows have one shape. A top-level `if` or `switch` in a row makes SwiftUI evaluate every row to
   count them: wrap it in a `VStack`, or filter before `ForEach`. No `AnyView` in rows.
5. No `View.if { }` helper. Vary the modifier's value (`.opacity(isOn ? 1 : 0.5)`).
6. `.task` and `.task(id:)`, never `onAppear { Task { } }`. A `.task(id:)` restarts and cancels
   itself when the id changes, which makes debouncing free.
7. Format in the view: `Text(date, format: .dateTime.day().month())`,
   `Text(price, format: .currency(code: "INR"))`. Don't store formatters.
8. Attach sheets, pickers and file importers once, at the screen, never on each row.

## Navigation and presentation

Details: `references/navigation.md`.

- One `NavigationStack(path:)` per tab, each with its own `@Observable` router holding `path` and
  `sheet`, injected with `.environment(router)`. `navigationDestination(for: Destination.self)` is
  registered once per stack.
- Value-based links only: `NavigationLink(value:)`, or `router.navigate(to:)` from a button. Never
  `NavigationLink(destination:)`.
- A pushed screen doesn't inherit the environment of the screen that pushed it. Pass ids, and share a
  multi-page flow's model through an environment store keyed by id.
- `.sheet(item:)` with one `Identifiable` enum per screen, not several `isPresented` flags. Sheets
  close themselves with `@Environment(\.dismiss)`.
- Destructive actions use `confirmationDialog` attached to their button. Alerts only when something
  blocks.
- Sheet and toolbar buttons use roles: `Button(role: .confirm)`, `.cancel`, `.close`. A custom Close
  or Back goes in `.cancellationAction`.
- Work that needs an account asks for sign-in and continues: `if !(await router.signIn()) { return }`.
- Deep links and universal links map web paths to destinations in one place; reset private screens
  when the account changes.

## Concurrency (Swift 6.2)

Details: `references/concurrency.md`.

- Read the build settings for the module first: language mode, default isolation, approachable
  concurrency flags. A missing `@MainActor` may already be implicit.
- In a main-actor module, your own nonisolated async functions run on the caller's actor. Mark
  CPU-heavy work (decoding big payloads, image processing) `@concurrent`. Plain network I/O already
  suspends and doesn't need it.
- No `Task.detached`, no `DispatchQueue`, no `DispatchSemaphore`, no `MainActor.run` where the code is
  already main-actor. `Task.sleep(for:)`, never `nanoseconds:`.
- Cancellation isn't an error. Catch `CancellationError` (or check `error.isCancellation`) first and
  return quietly; never show an alert or retry for it.
- Never swallow a user action's error with `try?` or a bare `Task { try await … }`. Show it inline.
- After any `await` inside an actor, re-check state. Never force-unwrap what you read before it.
- `Mutex` for small shared state in nonisolated code. `@unchecked Sendable` is not a fix.
- Delegate callbacks that arrive off the main actor with non-Sendable objects are `nonisolated`; copy
  out the `Sendable` part (a URL, an id) and hop.

## Design: native structure, Liquid Glass

Details: `references/design.md`.

- System structure and controls: tab bar, toolbars, sheets, menus, lists, search, `ShareLink`. They
  get Liquid Glass for free. Semantic colours, light and dark, Dynamic Type.
- Custom glass only on controls and navigation, never on content. Variants are `.regular`, `.clear`
  and `.identity`; there is no `.prominent`. `.glassEffect(...)` goes last in the chain.
  `.interactive()` only on things you can tap. Group nearby glass in one `GlassEffectContainer`.
- Custom bars use `.safeAreaBar(edge:)`, not a `ZStack` overlay with guessed padding. Never put an
  unbounded horizontal `ScrollView` in a top `safeAreaBar`; it grows to fill the screen.
- Hero images under bars and sidebars use `.backgroundExtensionEffect()`, once per screen.
- Toolbar items have a title and a symbol: `Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up")`.
  Use semantic placements (`.cancellationAction`, `.confirmationAction`, `.primaryAction`). On iOS 27
  overflow goes in `ToolbarOverflowMenu`, never a hand-made ellipsis `Menu`.
- `.font(.custom(name, size:, relativeTo:))` for brand fonts so they scale. `.italic()` does nothing on
  a font without an italic face; use the oblique face.

## Wide screens and iPhone Duo

- Decide wide layouts by the container (`onGeometryChange`: at least 600 pt, or wider than tall) or
  by size class, never by idiom or orientation. Test `== .regular`, never `!= .compact`.
- On screens with text input decide by width only. The keyboard changes the height, and a layout that
  flips under the cursor steals focus.
- Even grid column counts and 50/50 splits when wide, so a fold falls between panes.
- Selection and navigation state live above any size-dependent branch. Never switch between
  `TabView` and `NavigationSplitView` on size class; it destroys navigation state.
- The inner display can host two windows: take app-wide handoffs (a notification tap) once.
- iOS 27.1 fold APIs (`reservedRegions`, `ArrangementView`) go behind `#available(iOS 27.1, *)`.

## Models and decoding

Details: `references/data.md`.

- Keep the backend's field names (`CodingKeys` only for snake_case). Optional unless always sent.
- Status-like strings decode as a lenient enum with an `unknown` case. Lists of things people typed
  into the backend decode lossily: a bad item is dropped, not the screen.
- One type each for image references and for date-time triples the backend sends as strings.
- Comment the unit on every amount (rupees or paisa, dollars or cents).
- Count text lengths the way the server does: Python's `len()` counts Unicode scalars
  (`text.unicodeScalars.count`), not Swift `Character`s.
- Sign out only on the server's own refusal of the token. Never on no signal, a timeout, 5xx, 429 or
  a captive portal.

## Tests

Details: `references/testing.md`.

- Swift Testing for unit tests (`import Testing` only in test targets), XCTest for UI tests.
- Struct suites, `init()` for setup, no `test` prefix, `@Suite` only to name or add traits.
- `let x = try #require(optional)`; `#expect(throws: SpecificError.case)`.
- Test `@Observable` models directly, not views. Use a stub server per test, never the live network.
- Every response has a fixture and a decoding test. A bug fix has a test that failed first.

## UX defaults

Unless the project says otherwise:

- Errors inline where they happened. No toasts. Success is the screen changing plus a haptic
  (`.sensoryFeedback`).
- `textContentType` on every field (`.username` on email, `.newPassword`, `.oneTimeCode`) and the
  right keyboard.
- Ask for permissions in context (notifications after the first booking, never at launch).
- Buttons have text even when shown as icons (`.labelStyle(.iconOnly)`), and tap targets are at
  least 44 pt.

## Reviewing SwiftUI code

Report `file:line`, the rule, and a before and after snippet, most severe first:

1. Crashes and data loss: optional-chained `@Observable` writes, force unwraps after `await`,
   continuations resumed twice or never, sign-out on network errors.
2. State ownership: non-private `@State`, models created in `body` or `let`, parent input copied into
   `@State`, `@AppStorage` in a model.
3. Identity: unstable `ForEach` ids, rows with changing shape, `AnyView` rows.
4. Concurrency: swallowed errors, cancellation shown as failure, `Task.detached`, blanket
   `@MainActor` or `@unchecked Sendable`.
5. Navigation: `NavigationLink(destination:)`, several sheet flags, sheets attached to rows.
6. Accessibility, then deprecated APIs.

During feature work, finish the requested change and offer unrelated modernization in one line at the
end. Don't rewrite views you weren't asked to touch.

## References

| Read | When |
| --- | --- |
| `references/state.md` | `@State`, `@Observable`, bindings, environment, SDK 27 state init |
| `references/views.md` | composition, lists, identity, performance, accessibility, localization |
| `references/navigation.md` | routers, tabs, sheets, alerts, deep links, sign-in gates |
| `references/concurrency.md` | Swift 6.2 isolation, tasks, actors, Sendable, compiler errors |
| `references/design.md` | Liquid Glass, toolbars, iOS 27, iPhone Duo, widgets |
| `references/data.md` | Codable models, lenient decoding, the API client, sessions, caches |
| `references/testing.md` | Swift Testing, stub servers, fixtures |
| `references/modern-api.md` | old API to current API table |
