skills.name: plan-doc
skills.summary: Writes a plan as one clean HTML doc that leads with the recommendation and lists everything that changes.
skills.description: Write a plan as one clean, self-contained HTML document that people can read, review and approve. It leads with the recommendation, says in plain words what happens when it ships, lists every file, migration, template and env var that changes, and ends with open questions that each carry a recommended answer. House design with light and dark themes, hairlines instead of cards, one purple accent, phone-friendly, no build step and no network. Use when the user asks for a plan doc, design doc, proposal, RFC, one-pager, scope doc, migration or rollout plan, a progress or audit report, or to "write up the plan" for teammates, clients or later. For an interactive pre-coding approval gate built from a JSON model, use blueprint instead.
skills.body:
Write the plan as a document a busy person can read in three minutes and answer with "yes". One
`.html` file: it opens in any browser, survives being sent over chat, and can be published as an
artifact when the session has a tool for that.

`<skill-dir>` below is the folder holding this file. Claude Code exposes it as `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`.

## Use it or skip it

Use it when the plan will be read by someone other than you right now: a teammate, a client, the
user tomorrow. Typical asks: "write up the plan", "make a design doc", "scope this", "proposal for X",
"plan the migration", "status of each issue".

Skip it for a one-step change, or when the user wants the plan in chat. If they want a code-level
approval gate with diffs, playgrounds and annotations, that's `blueprint`.

## Workflow

1. **Research first. Planning is read-only.** Read the real code, schemas, configs and docs. Name
   actual files, functions, tables and env vars. Don't edit source, and don't run builds, tests or
   deploys while planning unless the user asks.
2. **Decide before you write.** Pick the recommendation. Plan it in one go; split into stages only if
   risk forces it, and say what forces it. Decide what's out of scope. Anything you can't decide
   becomes an open question with a recommended answer.
3. **Scaffold.**
   ```bash
   python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/plandoc.py new "Webhook retries" --out plans/
   ```
   It copies `assets/template.html` to `plans/webhook-retries.html` and fills the title, date,
   author, repo and branch from git. Use `--out` with a `.html` path to choose the exact file.
4. **Fill it.** Replace every `[[...]]` placeholder. Pull optional blocks (decisions, risks, status,
   diagram, out of scope, timeline) from `references/components.md`, in the order listed there.
   Delete the guidance comments as you go.
5. **Check.**
   ```bash
   python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/plandoc.py check plans/webhook-retries.html
   ```
   Fix every error. Fix warnings unless you have a reason. If the `unslop` skill sits next to this
   one, `check` also scans the prose. Treat its findings as edits to make.
6. **Hand it over.** Give the absolute path, the recommendation in one line, and what you need from
   the user. Presenting the doc is the approval request. Don't ask "does this look good?" separately.
   Don't start the work until they approve.
7. **Keep it current.** On feedback or scope change, edit the same file, move the status pill
   (`draft`, `in-review`, `approved`, `in-progress`, `done`, `dropped`) and add a changelog line.
   The doc is the source of truth, not the chat. Re-read it before big implementation steps.

## What makes it good

- **Recommendation first.** One call, stated plainly, with what you need from the reader. The user
  tends to reply "what would you recommend?", so answer that before they ask.
- **Plain words, short points.** "What happens when this ships" is written for someone who won't
  read the code: what users see, what changes in production, what could break.
- **Complete inventory.** The changes table lists every file, migration, template, env var, cron,
  queue and dependency the work touches. Nothing hidden behind "and related files".
- **Grounded.** Real paths in `<code>`. Real numbers or none. Secrets redacted (`rzp_live_•••`).
- **Every question has a default.** "Recommended: X, because Y" so the reader can just say yes.
- **Lean.** A short plan is a good plan. No filler sections, no single-step plans, no invented
  timeline. Delete any optional block that would hold one line of nothing.
- **Unslopped.** No em dashes, no hype, no `robust` or `seamless`, no closing flourish. Say what a
  thing does and stop. The `unslop` skill's rules apply to every sentence.

## Design rules

The template carries the house style. Keep it consistent across docs:

- One reading column, left-aligned text, about 70 characters wide. Sections split by hairlines.
- No cards, shadows, gradients, rounded panels or tinted boxes (code blocks excepted).
- Purple marks the recommendation and nothing else. Status colors (green, amber, red) only on tags
  and the status pill.
- Hierarchy comes from size, weight and spacing. Labels are lowercase mono, never uppercase eyebrows.
- Body text 17px, line height around 1.6. Readability wins over density.
- Light and dark both work: every color is a token on `:root`, redefined in the two dark blocks.
  Never write a color literal in a component rule.
- Works at phone width, offline, and in print. No web fonts; the system stacks are deliberate.
- Title is the plan's name in two to five words ("Webhook retries", "Hosting tab scope"). No
  "Plan:" prefix, no explanation after a dash or colon. The lede explains.

To change the house style, edit `assets/template.html` (tokens first), not one output file.

## Publishing as an artifact

When the session has an artifact publishing tool and the doc is meant for other people, offer to
publish it, or publish it if the user asked for a link. Those hosts wrap the page in their own
skeleton, so publish the fragment:

```bash
python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/plandoc.py fragment plans/webhook-retries.html
# writes plans/webhook-retries.artifact.html: no doctype, html, head or body tags; mermaid loader removed
```

Keep the `.html` as the source. Regenerate the fragment after each edit and republish to the same
URL. Without such a tool, the local file is the deliverable.

skills.name: pr-babysit
skills.summary: Babysits an open PR: CI, review bots, reviewers, a stale base. A bundled watcher wakes the agent once per real event.
skills.description: Looks after an open pull request until it's ready. Watches CI and review bots with a bundled watcher that wakes the agent once per real event, checks each finding against the code, fixes the real ones, answers the false ones with a reason, reruns flaky jobs once, keeps the branch current with its base, and stops when the PR is ready for a human. Use when the user says pr-babysit, babysit, watch or mind this PR, get it green, or deal with the review bots. Merges only when told to.
skills.body:
Keep a PR moving while nobody watches it: CI, review bots, reviewers and the base branch. Fix what
breaks, answer what's wrong, keep the PR at its original size, and leave the merge to a human.

`<skill-dir>` below is the folder holding this file. Claude Code exposes it as `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`.

Needs an authenticated `gh` and `python3`.

## Start

1. Find the PR: the number or URL the user gave, else `gh pr view --json number,url,headRefName`
   for the current branch. Note the base branch and how the repo merges (recent merged PRs).
2. Handle what's already there before waiting: failed checks, unanswered review comments, a stale
   branch.
3. Start the watcher. One watcher per PR, never your own `sleep` loop.

## The watcher

```bash
python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/pr_watch.py <pr-number-or-url> [--until ready|green|any]
```

It prints one line per event and exits on its own:

| Exit | Means | Do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `--until` met, or merged | check readiness yourself, then hand off |
| 1 | needs action: check failed, conflict, behind, unresolved threads, closed | act, push, start it again |
| 2 | bad input, or another watcher already has this PR | read stderr; don't start a second one |
| 3 | timed out with nothing to do (55 min by default) | start it again |

- `ready` (the default): required checks green, not behind, no unresolved review threads, and each
  review bot that reviewed this PR before has reviewed the latest push (or 15 minutes passed).
- `green`: required checks only, for repos without review bots.
- `any`: wake on the first event.

In Claude Code, run it under the **Monitor** tool with an hour's timeout so each line wakes you.
Without a monitor, run it as one blocking command with a long timeout. Start it again after every
push, after you handle an exit 1, and after a resume. It remembers what it already reported.

When an event needs nothing from you, go back to waiting without a message. Never post or say "still
waiting".

## Handling events

Only act on checks and comments newer than the latest push.

**A failed check.** Read the log (`gh run view <run-id> --log-failed`). Decide whether the failure
is the change's fault or the infrastructure's:

- Yours: fix it, prove the fix locally where you can, push.
- A flake (network timeout, runner died, a test that fails on main too): rerun once with
  `gh run rerun <run-id> --failed`. A second failure is real until shown otherwise. Say which it was.

**A review comment or bot finding.** Check it against the source before touching code. Bots are
useful and often wrong.

- Real and in scope: the smallest fix. Prefer the fix that deletes or narrows code.
- Real but out of scope: reply that it's a follow-up and list it in your report.
- Wrong: reply with the reason and the evidence (file:line, a test, output), then resolve the thread.
- Never resolve a human reviewer's thread you disagreed with. Reply and leave it for them.

Replies are short: the conclusion, then the evidence. No thanks-for-the-review filler. Follow the
repo's or user's rule on marking agent-written comments.

**Advisory bots** (CodeRabbit and others the repo treats as optional): treat their findings like any
other, but never hold the PR for them.

**Behind or conflicting.** Fetch, rebase onto the base, resolve conflicts by the PR's intent and the
base's newer rules, rerun the focused checks, push with
`git push --force-with-lease=<branch>:<sha you last saw>`. Never a bare `--force`.

## Keep it the size it was

Review loops grow PRs one cheap-looking fix at a time. Fix real bugs in the case the PR is for.
Decline the rest with a one-line reason and list them as follow-ups: tests nobody needs, guards for
cases that can't happen, extra compatibility, tiny performance wins. If the diff grew, cut before you
push.

## Stop

Stop when the watcher exits 0 and you've confirmed on the latest head:

- every change since the last proof is proven,
- required checks are green,
- review bots have finished and each finding is fixed or answered,
- no human review is requesting changes,
- the branch is current with its base and GitHub says it's mergeable.

Then report: the PR link, the final head, what you fixed, what you declined and why, flakes you
rerun, and anything left for a human.

**Never merge** unless the user asked for it in this task (or invoked `pr-merge`). Never use
`--admin` or bypass branch protection.

If another PR makes this one obsolete, stop watching and tell the user. Close it only if they said
so.

## Rate limits

`gh pr view` and `gh pr checks` use GraphQL; the watcher mostly uses REST, which has its own limit.
If GraphQL runs out, read PRs with `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n>` and checks with
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs`. Check with
`gh api rate_limit --jq .resources.graphql`, and wait for the reset with one background command
rather than retrying in a loop.

skills.name: pr-merge
skills.summary: pr-ready, then merges once every gate passes, never around branch protection.
skills.description: Takes a change all the way to a merged pull request with nobody watching. Runs the pr-ready workflow (finish, prove, second-model review, file, look after CI and bots), then merges once the merge gate passes, using the repo's merge method and never bypassing branch protection. Asking for pr-merge is permission to run the checks the proof needs and to merge this one PR. Use only when the user says pr-merge or ship and merge, or plainly asks for an unattended run that ends merged.
skills.body:
Everything `pr-ready` does, then merge once the gate passes. The user asked for this because they
want the change finished and merged without coming back to it.

Read the `pr-ready` skill and follow its steps, proof rules, filing rules, readiness gate and asking
rules. An explicit pr-merge request grants everything pr-ready grants, without a separate request.
The differences are below and win over pr-ready's.

If the user didn't clearly ask for this, don't assume permission to merge.

## The extra grant

Merge this task's PR once the merge gate passes. Nothing else changes: no other PRs, no pushes to
the default branch, no `--admin`, no bypassing branch protection or rulesets.

## Merge gate

pr-ready's readiness gate, plus:

- Right before merging, `git fetch` and check the live PR again. Never merge when it's behind or
  conflicting, or when base commits that landed after the last green run touch this PR's files.
  Rebase, push, wait for green again.
- Merge with the method the repo uses. Check the allowed methods (`gh repo view --json
  mergeCommitAllowed,squashMergeAllowed,rebaseMergeAllowed`) and how recent PRs were merged.
- If the repo uses a merge queue or auto-merge, use it and stay until GitHub reports the PR merged.
- An automated review asking for "human review" can be set aside when your proof covers the whole
  diff and no human has asked for changes. A human's request for changes cannot.
- If required approvals are missing, you can't merge. Stop at pr-ready's handoff with the
  verdict **Waiting on a human review**.

## After the merge

- Confirm it: `gh pr view <n> --json state,mergeCommit`.
- Delete the remote branch only if the repo does that for merged PRs.
- Stop any PR watcher still running.

## Report

Lead with **Merged** and the merge commit, then pr-ready's report items: the PR link, proof,
review and bot outcomes, decisions made for the user, and follow-ups. If you stopped before merging,
lead with the reason, as pr-ready's report does.

skills.name: pr-ready
skills.summary: Takes a change to a ready-to-merge PR with nobody watching: proves it, gets it reviewed, files it, babysits it. You merge.
skills.description: Takes a change all the way to a pull request that's ready to merge, with nobody watching. Finishes the change on a branch, proves it with evidence observed in the session, gets a second model's review, files a short PR that leads with the problem, looks after CI and review bots until the PR is ready, and stops there for the user to merge. Asking for pr-ready is permission to run the builds, tests and device checks the proof needs. Use only when the user says pr-ready or ready PR, or plainly asks for an unattended run to a ready PR. For a run that also merges, use pr-merge.
skills.body:
Take a change from where it is to a pull request that's ready to merge, then stop. The user merges.

The user asked for this because they aren't watching. Your updates and your final message
won't be read until long after you stop. You own the work from where it is now to a PR that is ready
to merge, and you stop there.

If the user didn't clearly ask for this, don't assume this much autonomy.

## What it grants

For this task only:

- Create a branch, commit, push it, and open a PR.
- Rebase the PR's own branch and push it with `--force-with-lease`.
- Run the builds, tests, simulators, devices, app launches and screenshots the proof needs, without
  asking first. This replaces "ask before building" or "leave testing to me" rules in `AGENTS.md`
  or `CLAUDE.md` for this task.

Rules about *how* to test still apply: the device the project names, one Gradle build at a time,
the project's test command, no `clean`. The grant removes the asking step, nothing else. It doesn't
cover merging, closing PRs, force-pushing other branches, production systems, deleting data, or
anything outside the repo. It doesn't bypass a harness approval prompt either.

## Steps

1. **Finish the change.** Do what the user asked with the smallest change that works. Fix the case
   that happened, not every case that could. If you're on the default branch, branch first.
2. **Prove it.** Evidence for every change in the diff. See Proof.
3. **Get a second read.** Use the `cross-model-review` skill if installed. Otherwise give a fresh subagent the
   diff and the intent (not your conclusions) and ask for bugs only. Fix real findings, decline the
   rest with a reason.
4. **Commit** in the repo's style: look at `git log` and any commit rules in the project's docs. One
   commit per logical change. No AI co-author or "generated with" trailers unless the repo asks for
   them.
5. **File the PR.** See Filing.
6. **Look after it** with the `pr-babysit` skill until it's ready: CI, review bots, reviewers, the
   base branch. Prove each fix before pushing it.
7. **Hand off** at the readiness gate with the report below.

Stay active from step 1 to step 7. If you end your turn while checks or bots are pending, the work
stops, because nobody will prompt you again. Wait with pr-babysit's watcher so an event wakes you.

## Proof

Proof is evidence you observed in this session: command output, a reproduction, a screenshot. Use
the most direct proof the change allows:

- Reproduce the original failure, apply the fix, and watch the same reproduction pass.
- Run the checks CI runs (typecheck, lint, tests) for the touched area.
- Add one focused test that fails without the fix, when the behaviour has none and the repo has a
  test setup.
- For UI and runtime behaviour, run the app and look at the change. Green mocked tests don't prove
  the experience works. Attach screenshots to the PR when they help and you can upload them.

If you can't find a way to prove a change, you don't have full confidence. Ask (see Asking).

## Filing

- Check whether a PR already exists for the branch (`gh pr view`). Update it instead of opening a
  second one.
- Rebase onto the latest default branch first, and read the final diff against it. It should match
  the goal and nothing else.
- Title: the repo's convention (titles often become merge commits). Say why it matters, not which
  mechanism changed: "Stop signing people out on flaky networks", not "Handle 5xx in AuthInterceptor".
- Description: the problem in one or two plain sentences from the user's point of view, then the fix
  in a sentence or two, then one line on how you proved it. No inventory of every file touched. If
  the `unslop` skill is installed, follow its PR genre rules.
- Before submitting, check the title, body, quotes and screenshots for secrets and private details.
- Open a real PR, not a draft, so review bots run. If `gh pr create` hits the GraphQL rate limit,
  use REST: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls -f title=... -f head=... -f base=... -F body=@<file>`.

## Readiness gate

Ready means all of these hold on the latest head:

- Your proof covers every change in the diff, including fixes made during review.
- Required checks are green.
- Review bots have finished, and every finding is fixed or answered with a reason.
- No human review is requesting changes.
- The branch is up to date with its base and GitHub reports it mergeable.

Before handing off, fetch and recheck the live PR: open, not a draft, not set to auto-merge. Disable
auto-merge and leave any merge queue if either is on, and say so. Never merge, enable auto-merge,
enter a merge queue or push to the default branch.

## Asking

A question in a normal message goes unseen, and the thread looks finished. Ask with the harness's
question tool so the thread shows it's waiting (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code,
`request_user_input` in Codex). Put everything in the question: the PR link, what blocks you, the
options with your recommendation first.

Ask only when you can't go on alone:

- You can't prove the change.
- The gate can't pass and you can't fix that yourself.
- The next step is outside the grant.
- The goal is ambiguous in a way that changes the result.
- Another PR makes this one obsolete.

Decide everything else yourself with sensible defaults and list those decisions in the report. If
there's no question tool or no answer comes, take the safe path: leave the PR as it is and start
your final message with the question.

## Report

Lead with the verdict: **Ready to merge** (the gate passed), **Waiting on a human review**
(confirm that's the only blocker), or **Blocked** (what blocks it, what you tried, what's needed).
Then:

- the PR link and final head,
- how you proved it,
- what the reviewer and the bots found, and what you did about each,
- decisions you made on the user's behalf,
- remaining risks or follow-ups,
- that the PR is open and unmerged.

skills.name: pr-revive
skills.summary: Revives a stale PR: decides REBASE, REWRITE or CLOSE, then rebases it safely.
skills.description: Revives a stale pull request and decides whether it still belongs. Reads the PR's intent, checks what changed on the base since it branched (replacements, moved code, new rules), and gives one verdict, REBASE (rebase, test, push), REWRITE (the goal holds but the code is stale) or CLOSE (superseded or no longer worth it, closed only with the user's OK), with evidence. Rebases with range-diff checks and a lease-protected push. Never merges or closes. Use when the user says pr-revive, revive, rebase or update an old PR, bring this branch up to date, or asks whether a stale PR still makes sense.
skills.body:
Bring back the idea, not just the branch. A clean rebase doesn't prove a
PR still belongs in the product.

## Guardrails

- Fetch first: the PR's head, its base, and any branch related to the work.
- Existing changes in the working tree belong to the user. If the tree is dirty or busy with other
  work, use a disposable worktree (`git worktree add`).
- A pr-revive request allows rebasing and updating the PR's branch. It doesn't allow merging, closing,
  changing the base branch, or widening the scope.
- Push a rebased branch only with `--force-with-lease=<branch>:<head sha you recorded>`. Never a
  bare `--force`.
- Don't post a PR comment unless the user asked for one.

## 1. Pin down the intent

Record the PR's URL, state, base, head repository and branch, head SHA, author, checks and review
state. Read the title, body, linked issues, commits, review threads and the full diff. Write the
smallest goal the PR was trying to reach before you judge how it reached it.

Record the merge base, so the PR's own changes and the base's later changes can be compared
separately.

## 2. See what changed around it

Read the commits and diffs that landed on the base since the PR branched. Search merged and open PRs
when titles, paths or behaviour suggest a replacement or a competing fix. Look past overlapping
lines:

- Has the same user-facing problem already been solved another way?
- Did APIs, types, schemas, dependencies or module boundaries change under it?
- Do both sides now claim the same behaviour or rule?
- Was the code it changes deleted, moved or deliberately simplified?
- Would landing it bring back old behaviour, or create two ways to do one thing?
- Is the original benefit still worth the upkeep?

No conflicts in Git doesn't mean current.

## 3. Pick a verdict before pushing anything

| Verdict | When | Then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| REBASE | the goal still matters and the implementation is still the right shape | rebase, resolve, test, push |
| REWRITE | the goal still matters, but a mechanical rebase would keep the wrong implementation | describe the smallest believable rewrite and stop, unless the user also asked you to do it |
| CLOSE | superseded, obsolete, pointed the wrong way, or not worth its cost | cite the evidence (the PR or commit that replaced it, the code that moved) and stop. Don't rebase it, and don't close it without the user's say-so |

Be willing to recommend CLOSE. Age isn't evidence, and effort already spent isn't a reason to keep a PR.

## 4. Rebase without losing the point (REBASE)

1. Make a local branch or disposable worktree at the recorded head.
2. Rebase its commits onto the freshly fetched base.
3. Resolve each conflict by the PR's intent and the base's newer rules. A conflict that exposes a
   product or architecture disagreement means stop and reconsider the verdict, not guess.
4. Compare the series before and after with `git range-diff <old-base>..<old-head> <new-base>..HEAD`,
   then read the final diff. Nothing intended should vanish, and nothing already on the base should
   come back.
5. Run the repo's focused checks for the touched area. Separate real failures from ones that already
   fail on the base or come from infrastructure.
6. Push with the lease tied to the recorded head. If the lease fails, someone pushed: fetch and
   reassess, never overwrite.

If the user wants it carried to ready, hand over to the `pr-babysit` skill after the push.

## Report

Lead with **REBASE**, **REWRITE** or **CLOSE** and the reason in one sentence. Then:

- what changed on the base that matters,
- conceptual conflicts, or that there were none,
- the rebase and push result, if you did them,
- checks run and their results,
- what's left to decide, with the PR link.

Keep what you observed apart from what you judge, and say what you couldn't verify.

skills.name: replay
skills.summary: Turns a finished diff into an interactive review and shows where the work drifted from its blueprint.
skills.description: Turn a finished diff, PR, branch, or commit range into ONE self-contained interactive HTML replay of the change — outcome narrative, file map with change flags, annotated diffs you can flip between split/unified with word-level highlights, a pan/zoom architecture diagram whose nodes click through to the relevant diff, a risk/blast-radius heatmap, and a PLAN-VS-REALITY DRIFT tracker that flags where the code deviated from the original plan (as-planned / changed / skipped / unplanned). Plus reviewer annotations that export back to the agent. Zero dependencies: no MCP, no server, no account; works offline and is shareable as a single file. Use to summarize completed work for review at a higher level than line-by-line, before or alongside a PR. (Prism suite; pairs with `blueprint`.)
skills.body:
Produce a **replay** of completed work as a single self-contained HTML file: a plan built *from*
a diff, not toward one. It helps a reviewer understand the **shape** of a change — outcome, file map,
the few diffs that matter, risk, and how reality compared to the plan — before they dive into raw code.

The diffs are **interactive**: split/unified toggle, word-level intra-line highlights, collapsible
context, copy buttons; the architecture diagram pans/zooms and its nodes jump to the diff they describe.

Like `blueprint`, the artifact is one HTML file with the recap model embedded as JSON. No MCP, no
server, no account. Commit it next to the PR, or send it as one file.

## The standout: plan-vs-reality drift

If an original `blueprint` artifact exists for this work (a `*-model.json` with `"kind":"plan"`, or the
plan the user references), **load it and compute drift**: walk its `steps`/`decision` blocks against what
the diff actually did, and emit a `drift` block classifying each item as `as-planned`, `changed`,
`skipped`, or `added` (unplanned). This accountability layer is the reason to reach for this skill over a
plain PR description. If there is no prior plan, skip the `drift` block — don't fabricate one.

## Workflow

1. **Collect the diff from real sources.** Use the actual change set — don't infer it:
   ```bash
   git diff main...HEAD                 # branch vs base
   git show <sha>                       # single commit
   git diff <base>..<head> --stat       # file map + churn
   gh pr diff <number>                  # a GitHub PR
   ```
   Read the touched files for context. Every block must derive mechanically from this diff —
   real paths, fields, methods, and before/after text only.

2. **Read the block catalog.** Open `references/BLOCKS.md` for the authoritative vocabulary and schema.
   Author from it, not memory.

3. **Author the model JSON** (`{ "kind":"recap", ... }`). Canonical recap shape, top to bottom:
   - `metrics` — files changed, +/− lines, new deps, risk at a glance.
   - `summary` (top-level field) — 1–3 paragraph outcome narrative: what shipped and why it matters.
   - `drift` — plan-vs-reality, **if a prior plan exists** (see above).
   - `diagram` — an **auto architecture diagram**: derive a Mermaid flow/sequence from the real
     import/call relationships the diff introduces or changes (not hand-waved boxes).
   - `filetree` — every changed file with `change` flag and `plus`/`minus` churn; one-line `note` on the
     non-obvious ones.
   - `tabs` (label "Key changes") — 3–8 focused `diff` blocks, each with a `note` saying *why* the hunk
     matters. Show the lines that explain the change, not the whole patch.
   - `risk` — blast-radius heatmap: score each touched file (churn × fan-in/out × test-coverage gaps ×
     how critical the path is), with reasons and mitigation.
   - `datamodel` / `api` — only if schema or endpoints changed.
   - `decision` — any non-obvious choice the diff embodies, with rationale and reversibility.
   - `questions` — anything left open for the reviewer.

   **Lean is not thin.** Keep it scannable, but include enough real diff/file evidence that the reader
   trusts it. A recap that's all headlines and no code is a defect.

4. **Build the artifact.**
   ```bash
   python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/build.py recap-model.json -o RECAP.html
   python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/build.py recap-model.json -o RECAP.html --fetch-mermaid   # offline diagram rendering
   ```

5. **Surface it.** Give the user the absolute path to the `.html`. It opens in any browser, no server.

6. **Annotation round-trip.** Reviewers turn on **✎ Annotate**, click blocks to leave notes, then
   **⧉ Copy** / **⬇ JSON** to hand them back. Read the notes; if they require code changes, make them and
   regenerate the recap from the new diff so the artifact stays true to reality.

## Rules

- **Grounding is mechanical.** Real paths, fields, methods, before/after text — derived from the diff,
  never inferred or invented. Read the files.
- **Redact secrets** in every block and prose (`sk-•••`, `<redacted>`).
- **Drift must be honest.** Surface skipped and unplanned work, not just the wins — that's the whole point.
- **A recap reflects reality.** If code changes after review, regenerate from the new diff; don't hand-edit
  the output `.html`. When the renderer looks wrong, fix `scripts/template.html`, not one artifact.

skills.name: unslop
skills.summary: Rewrites text so it reads like a person wrote it. A bundled scanner flags AI tells by line in Markdown, HTML, commit messages and diffs.
skills.description: Rewrite text so it reads like a person wrote it. Strips AI tells (puffery, filler, praise, stacked hedges, em dashes, bold-label bullets, emoji headers, cute closers, AI attribution trailers) while keeping facts, code, numbers and the author's voice. Use when the user says unslop, deslop, "sounds too AI", "make it human", humanize or tighten, or asks to clean up a README, docs page, PR description, commit message, changelog, email, Slack message, blog post, bio or portfolio copy. Also turns a voice-dictated draft into a clean message and audits only the lines a branch added. Ships a stdlib scanner that flags tells by line in Markdown, HTML, commit messages and diffs, and can block sloppy commits as a commit-msg hook.
skills.body:
Rewrite text so a careful person could have written it. Same facts, same stance, fewer words, no tells.
The target is text a reader trusts. Passing a detector is a side effect.

`<skill-dir>` below is the folder holding this file. Claude Code exposes it as `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`.

## Pick the mode

| The user gives you | Mode | You |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pasted text, "unslop this" | Rewrite | return the rewrite |
| a file, folder or glob | Files | edit in place, report counts before and after |
| "unslop this branch", "clean my docs changes" | Diff | touch only lines the branch added |
| a commit message, PR body, changelog | Ship | apply the genre rules in `references/genres.md` |
| a voice-dictated draft | Dictation | resolve self-corrections, drop fillers, keep their voice |
| "unslop yourself", "stop sounding like AI" | Session | apply these rules to your own replies from now on |

## Workflow

1. **Read all of it first.** Name the genre, the reader, and the one thing the text must get across.
   Open `references/genres.md` for that genre.
2. **Scan for an inventory.**
   ```bash
   python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/scan.py README.md docs/*.md       # Markdown or text
   python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/scan.py plan.html                  # HTML, visible text only
   pbpaste | python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/scan.py -                # pasted text
   git diff main...HEAD | python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/scan.py --diff -   # only added lines
   python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/scan.py --commit-msg msg.txt       # commit message checks
   python3 <skill-dir>/scripts/scan.py --dictation -              # speech fillers too
   ```
   The scanner catches word and phrase tells. It can't see empty sentences, padding, structure or rhythm.
   Read for those yourself with `references/patterns.md`.
3. **Rewrite in four passes.**
   1. *Cut.* Delete what says nothing: preambles, restated summaries, praise, sign-offs, "it's worth
      noting". If a paragraph can go with no loss, it goes.
   2. *Make it concrete.* Swap each puffed word for the plain word or the actual fact. Name the mechanism
      ("retries the Razorpay capture twice") instead of the feeling ("makes payments smoother").
   3. *Fix the shape.* Headings only where a reader navigates. Bullets only for parallel items. Bold
      almost never. A table when the same labels repeat.
   4. *Read it as the reader.* Vary sentence length. Join choppy fragments. Split anything you had to
      read twice.
4. **Verify.** Rescan: every high finding is gone or kept on purpose. Then check meaning: every fact,
   number, name, link, command and caveat from the original is still there.
5. **Report** in the format under Output.

## Never change

- Facts, numbers, dates, names, prices, versions, links, commands, code, error text, quoted words.
- What the author thinks. Change tone only when asked ("make it formal").
- Real uncertainty. One honest "probably" stays. Three stacked hedges become one.
- Anything inside code fences, inline code, or someone else's quote.

## Never invent

The fix for a vague claim is never a made-up specific. `significantly faster` with no number becomes
`faster`, not `3x faster`. `Experts agree` with no source gets cut, not cited. When a sentence needs a
fact you don't have, put `[TODO: number?]` in the file (Files mode) or list it under "Needs from you"
(Rewrite mode).

## Don't overcorrect

Slop has an opposite failure mode. Avoid these too:

- Telegraph style: dropped articles, arrows, "w/", stacks of fragments posing as sentences.
- Trading one tic for another, like turning every em dash into a colon or a semicolon. Most should
  become a period.
- Removing structure readers need: numbered setup steps, a reference table, a code sample.
- Curt instead of plain. Keep "please" and "thanks" where a person would say them.
- Restyling someone's voice. Lowercase stays lowercase; slang stays if it's theirs.
- Monotone rhythm. Five eight-word sentences in a row is its own tell.

## House style

These are this user's standing preferences. They apply unless the text's owner says otherwise.

- **No em dashes.** Not in prose, headings, UI copy or commit messages. Use a period, a comma or
  parentheses.
- **Say what it is or does in one short sentence, then stop.** No closing flourish, aphorism or
  `and that's the point`.
- **Nothing hyped.** No launch voice (`excited to announce`), no marketing adjectives, no `game-changer`.
- **No meta-framing.** No `in this post I'll`, `let me walk you through`, or openers that defend an
  earlier choice.
- **Plain technical register for blogs and portfolio copy.** First person, concrete about what was
  built, how, and what broke. Keep lowercase if the source is lowercase.
- **Simple words, short points** when the reader has to act. Lead with the recommendation.
- **Formal when the reader is a customer** (refund or policy emails) or when asked.
- **Commits.** Conventional prefix plus two or three words (`fix: refund retries`, `docs: install table`).
  No body unless the why isn't obvious from the diff. One commit per logical change.
- **PR descriptions.** Short. What changed, what to check, then stop.
- **No AI attribution.** Never a Claude co-author trailer, session trailer or "Generated with" line in
  commits or PRs.

## Dictation mode

The user often dictates. Their drafts have fillers ("uh", "I mean"), restarts, and inline corrections
("10 business templates, sorry, WhatsApp templates"). When cleaning one:

- Keep only the corrected phrase: "10 WhatsApp templates".
- Drop fillers and repeated words. Merge the restarts into one sentence.
- Fix a misheard word only when context makes the intended word certain. Otherwise mark it `[?]`.
- Keep their words, their order of points and their directness. Don't upgrade it into polished AI
  prose. It should sound like them on a good day.
- Don't add points they didn't make, and don't drop ones they did.

Run `scan.py --dictation -` on the draft to find every filler and correction before you start.

## Session mode

When told to unslop yourself, apply Never change, House style and every high-severity rule in
`references/patterns.md` to your own replies for the rest of the session. Don't announce it each time.

## Output

- **Rewrite.** The rewritten text first (fenced if they will copy it). Then at most three short lines:
  what kinds of things changed, and anything under "Needs from you". No itemized change log unless asked.
- **Files and Diff.** Edit in place. One line per file, e.g. `README.md: high 12 -> 0, medium 9 -> 2`,
  plus any tell you kept on purpose and why.
- **Ship.** The final message, ready to paste or commit.
- Never paste the original back.

## Scanner reference

| Flag | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `-` | read stdin (add `--html` if it's HTML) |
| `--diff` | input is a unified diff; scans added lines, and only comments in code files |
| `--commit-msg FILE` | skips `#` lines and the scissors tail; adds subject length, mood and period checks |
| `--dictation` | adds speech filler, self-correction and stutter rules |
| `--format json` | machine-readable findings, counts and score |
| `--min-severity medium` | hide low findings |
| `--strict [--max-score N]` | exit 1 on any high finding (or a score over N) |
| `--allow PHRASE`, `--disable RULE` | per-run exceptions |

Severity: **high** almost never survives a human edit. **Medium** is usually filler and sometimes
earned. **Low** is fine alone and a tell in bulk. The score is weighted findings per 100 words: under
1 is clean, under 3 light, under 8 heavy, above that slop.

**Project config.** A `.unslop.json` in the repo (found by walking up from the working directory)
holds house exceptions and extra rules:

```json
{
  "allow": ["robust"],
  "disable": ["exclamation"],
  "rules": [
    { "id": "old-name", "pattern": "\\boutworld\\b", "severity": "high", "hint": "it's fanpit.live now" }
  ]
}
```

**Suppressions.** `unslop:ignore` anywhere on a line skips it. `<!-- unslop:off -->` and
`<!-- unslop:on -->` skip a region, which is how a style guide can quote bad examples.

**Commit hook.** When the user asks for it, look at `.git/hooks/commit-msg` first and don't overwrite
an existing hook without asking. Then:

```bash
SCAN="$(cd <skill-dir> && pwd)/scripts/scan.py"
printf '#!/bin/sh\nexec python3 "%s" --commit-msg "$1" --strict\n' "$SCAN" > .git/hooks/commit-msg
```
